title: Introducing Cedar Multithreading: find the people who move the deal
summary: Build an account’s org chart from public evidence, research the people who matter, and refine the picture with conversations from your deals.
body_markdown:
You can know an account well and still be missing the person who can move the deal forward.


Your champion has explained the problem. The evaluation looks promising. But you still need to understand the organization around them: who owns the budget, who will influence the decision, and who else needs a reason to care. A contact list gives you names. It takes more work to understand how those people fit together and where your relationships are missing.


Today, we’re introducing Cedar’s multithreading workflow: org mapping, deep research, and deal context working together to help reps understand who to engage and prepare for that conversation.


## A request from the people doing the work


John at Warp described the problem before we showed him the feature. In the launch film, he asks whether Cedar could help him multithread: research the people around a contact, work out who is on their team, and help explain why another person should join the conversation.


The last part matters. Finding another email address is useful, but it doesn’t answer the question a buyer will ask: why are you bringing this person in?


A useful introduction connects someone’s role to the work already happening in the deal. It might bring an executive into a discussion about an initiative they own, or include the person responsible for implementing a proposed change. The rep needs enough context to make that connection credible.


That is the workflow we wanted to build. Start with the relationships you already have, understand the organization around them, and prepare a specific next step toward the people who matter to the purchase.


## Build an org chart from the clues companies leave


Companies rarely publish the exact org chart a seller needs. A team page may show the leadership group while leaving out the managers, specialists, and newer hires involved in your deal. Individual profiles can describe a role without telling you who someone reports to.


The clues are often there, spread across different places. Someone announces a new job. A manager posts about hiring for a particular team. Two people describe the same initiative. Tenure, previous positions, location, and public interactions can add context to those signals.


Cedar brings those clues together to infer an organization’s structure from publicly available information. The launch shows sources such as job postings, announcements, professional profiles, and comments on posts being used to build a more useful picture of the team.


This gives the rep a starting point for account planning without having to collect every clue manually. Research that would otherwise live across browser tabs can contribute to one picture of the people around a deal.


### Understand why a relationship was inferred


In the film, Cedar combines two LinkedIn posts to infer a reporting relationship. One person has posted about hiring founding account executives and sales development representatives in London. Another announces a new role, mentions that person, and describes looking forward to working together. Their location also aligns with the team being built.


Those details are more useful together than they are individually. A hiring post identifies a team and someone involved in building it. The new-hire announcement connects a particular person to that effort. Location adds another piece of context.


It is still an inference. The posts do not become an official reporting record just because the evidence fits. Their value is that they give the rep a reasoned hypothesis to work with and something concrete to confirm as the relationship develops.


That distinction keeps the map useful. It can guide the next question without pretending that public research reveals every internal relationship.


## Know who to engage, then research what matters to them


Once you have a clearer picture of the organization, the next problem is often the message.


An executive may be important to the purchase, but their title alone gives you little to say. The conversation your champion has been having may focus on day-to-day work. The economic buyer may care about the wider initiative, the consequences of leaving the problem unresolved, or how the proposed change fits their priorities.


Cedar’s deep research skill helps fill that gap. As shown in the launch, it can investigate public appearances, personal blogs, and other material that reveals what an executive has been discussing.


The purpose is to understand the person’s professional priorities well enough to connect the deal to them. A mention of a business initiative is useful when it helps explain why the problem your buyer described deserves attention. An unrelated personal detail adds little to that conversation.


### Turn research into a reason to talk


For example, imagine an executive has publicly discussed improving how their team scales. Your existing conversations show that manual work is slowing the team down. Those two pieces of information can help you prepare a message that connects the evaluation to an initiative the executive has already described.


The connection needs to be supported by what the executive said and what your buyer told you.


The advantage is that org mapping and research are part of the same job. Finding the right stakeholder leads into understanding their priorities, which leads into preparing a more relevant conversation. The rep gets help moving through the work rather than stopping at a list of names.


## Let conversations improve the map


Public information will never tell you everything about a buying organization. A new hire may not have announced their role. A person with an unremarkable title may be central to the decision. A senior executive may have an opinion about the evaluation that appears nowhere online.


Your conversations can reveal those details. Cedar updates the org chart and its relevant context as you learn more from prospects.


The launch gives two examples: a buyer mentioning someone in RevOps whose job has not been announced, and a conversation revealing the economic buyer’s sentiment. These are different kinds of information, but both change how a rep understands the account. One may add a person to the picture. The other may change the conversation the team needs to have.


This makes the chart more useful over the life of the deal. Public research establishes an initial view; the conversations you are already having help refine it. The account’s context can develop with the relationship instead of depending on a research document written before the first meeting.


It also helps preserve what the team has learned. A stakeholder’s relevance is easier to understand when it stays connected to the deal context that made them important.


## Put that context to work for the rep


The launch finishes by connecting org mapping to Cedar’s core agents. Together, they can help show how a deal is progressing toward the people with decision-making authority, surface proactive alerts in Slack, and prepare research and drafts for the next step.


That turns stakeholder research into ongoing deal work. A missing relationship can become something the rep needs to address. New information from a conversation can make the next action more specific. Research can support a draft that explains why another person’s involvement would be useful.


The rep still needs to navigate the buying relationship thoughtfully. A suggested stakeholder is a starting point for a conversation, and a draft needs to fit the situation. Cedar brings more of the relevant context and preparation into that decision.


The result is a connected workflow: understand the organization, identify the people you still need to engage, research their priorities, and keep improving the picture as the deal develops.
